t.en: In the prover, “it rains ∧ it is windy” means what the <part-ref to="part:gAnd"></part-ref> gate of <level-ref to="g-and"></level-ref> does: it rains, and it is windy.

<level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref> declared “and”, and the proof board gained two parts: <part-ref to="part:andI"></part-ref>, its one introduction rule, and <part-ref to="part:andE"></part-ref>, the elimination rule made from it, whose two outputs give the left and the right. Every connective has its introduction and elimination rules; a system of rules organised this way is called <wiki-ref to="natural"></wiki-ref>.

after.en: A sentence proved from no givens is a <wiki-ref to="theorem"></wiki-ref>: a tautology of the truth tables, here proved.

hint.en: Take it apart, then put it back together in the new order.
The proof you just made can move into a box whole: assume “it rains ∧ it is windy”.

t.en: This time nothing is given: “it rains ∧ it is windy → it is windy ∧ it rains” always holds.
